(2017, 2018) consider the case of transboundary pollu- tion, their analyses are limited to environmental subsidies under exogenous taxes or regulations. In studies on environmental industries and multiple policy instruments, when examining the welfare effects of one instrument, other instruments are often assumed to be exogenous.7 In this paper, the simultaneous choice of tax and subsidy policies is considered. This paper shows that, under transboundary pollution, non-cooperative emission taxes are lower than the Pigouvian level, whereas non-cooperative environmental subsidies are higher than the efficient level under imperfect competition. Although high subsidies mitigate the distortion of low taxes to some extent, the equilibrium level of pollution is inefficiently high. Thus, transboundary pollution reduces the effectiveness of environmental policies under non-cooperative policymaking.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Partnerships for the goals|Global sustainability regulation|Environmental policy frameworks_qna_001
nodes.label: Factual
nodes.question: What is the distinction between "soft" and "hard" policies in the context of environmental interventions?
nodes.answer: Soft" policies are relatively less intrusive and include measures like labelling, while "hard" policies are more intrusive and may involve rationing or banning products.

nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What does the socio-ecological systems (SES) framework focus on in relation to waste management?
nodes.answer: The SES framework focuses on examining waste dynamics within households and their interaction with the natural environment, incorporating social, political, and economic factors that influence ecological outcomes.
nodes.paragraph: This theory highlights the social, political and economic factors that influence ecological outcomes. Building on the foundations of social ecology theory, the socio-ecological systems (SES) framework provides a com- prehensive approach for examining waste dynamics within households, between households, and between household solid waste generators and the natural environment. This study explores waste management practices informed by local knowledge that support ecological system sustain- ability. The SES framework helps to identify key variables needed to understand both social and ecological systems, and how they interact with each other (Binder et al. 2013 , p. 15 of 20). By suggesting specific variables, the framework allows us to analyze the potential for sustainable develop- ment within these systems, providing a structured way to assess whether a social-ecological system can remain resil- ient and sustainable over time (Ostrom 2009, p. 420; Leslie et al. 2015, p. 5979). The SES framework has proven relevant in explaining sustainable outcomes in the management of forestry, fish- eries, and water resources (Bhatt et al. 2024; Binder et al.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Partnerships for the goals|Global sustainability regulation|Environmental policy frameworks_qna_003
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: How do studies on environmental policy categorize policies based on regulatory approaches?
nodes.answer: Studies on environmental policy categorize policies based on regulatory approaches into regulation (stick), economical means (carrot), and information (sermon) according to Vending (1998).

nodes.id: Subtopic:Governance|Partnerships for the goals|Global sustainability regulation|Environmental policy frameworks_qna_004
nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What challenges are associated with environmental regulations in the U.S.?
nodes.answer: Environmental regulations can be controversial and easily politicized.
nodes.paragraph: While we are interested in what sectors are covered by CAPs, we also seek to better understand the types of strategies employed. Here, we under - stand climate change as a collective action problem (Ostrom 2010 ; Hormio 2023 ) and thus define a strategy typology under policy mechanisms for solving collective action problems: rules, incentives, and norms (Young 2013 ). Each of these three policy tools present opportunities and challenges for city climate action. For instance, when an emissions source falls under a city S jurisdictional powers, new rules can be an efficient path towards rapid GHG reduction. However, environmental regulations can be controversial and easily politicized in the U.S. (Hanna and McDonald 2021 ; Basseches et al. 2022 ), and the majority of community emissions may originate from sectors that cities lack the power to control. In this case, incentives can become a popular option as they help guide but don t overtly control the behavior of private sector and civil society actors. On the other hand, cities require sufficient resources to offer powerful incen - tives, and high emitters must weigh whether an incentive program can adequately cover their costs to reduce emissions.

nodes.question: Are environmental permit systems widely adopted globally?
nodes.answer: Yes, environmental permit systems have been legally adopted in almost all countries in the world.

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: How are the SAFA guidelines organized?
nodes.answer: The SAFA guidelines are organized under the broader categories of environment, social, economy, and governance, which structure the results of the review.
nodes.paragraph: 2017). The SAFA guidelines (FAO 2014) provide a framework for assessing the benefits and trade-offs of agriculture and food system practices on different sustainability issues. The guidelines are organised under the broader categories of environment, social, economy and governance, which are used for structuring the results of the review. These are further distinguished into themes and sub-themes with for - mulated sustainability objectives and indicators to measure sustainability criteria. Over the last years, the guidelines have been used to study the impact of livestock systems in various contexts (Cammarata et al. 2021; P rez-Lombardini et al. 2021; Niloofar et al. 2023). The range and structure of indicators within SAFA provides an overarching reference point for structuring the analysis. Complementing the One Health concept, which under - lines the strong connection between animal and human health, the One Welfare approach relates the wellbeing of animals to that of humans and recognizes their intercon- nections with the environment (Pinillos et al. 2016). Con- sidering these interactions makes it possible to detect and capitalize on direct and indirect benefits of one dimension on the other and thereby enables a holistic way to increase both human and animal welfare on a global scale (ibid.).
